bullets: **Lord Byron (1788–1824)** was a Romantic poet, famous for his scandalous life and rebellious views. He later died while supporting Greek independence.
The poem appeared in **Hebrew Melodies (1815)**, a collection of lyrics set to Jewish tunes by the composer Isaac Nathan, meant to be sung.
1815 was the year of **Waterloo** and Napoleon’s fall. Many readers saw a parallel: a seemingly unstoppable conquering army humbled. Use this cautiously as a link.
Romantic interest in the **power of nature and the supernatural** over human ambition.

callouts.p: Because the poem was written to be sung, its galloping rhythm and simple couplets serve a musical purpose; this explains why the form is so regular even when describing mass death.

core.h: Context (AO3): the Bible, Byron and Napoleon
core.p: The poem retells **2 Kings 18–19** (also Isaiah 37): around 701 BC, King Sennacherib of Assyria besieged Jerusalem. King Hezekiah prayed, and ‘the angel of the Lord’ killed 185,000 Assyrian soldiers in one night. Sennacherib withdrew.

bullets: **Conflict type**: a military invasion ended by divine intervention; God vs human pride.
**Big message**: human military might is nothing compared with God; pride and aggression are punished.
**Perspective**: third-person, epic narrator: distant and dramatic.
core.p: The Assyrian army attacks like a wolf, gleaming in purple and gold. Like summer leaves at sunset, they look full of life; by morning they lie dead like autumn leaves. The Angel of Death breathed on them as they slept. A dead horse lies foaming; a dead rider lies rusting; the camp is silent. The widows of Assyria mourn, their idols are broken, and the might of the Gentile army has melted like snow at a glance from God.

bullets: **Contrast structure**: stanza 1 is the glamorous army; stanzas 3–5 are death; stanza 6 is the aftermath. The volta is inside stanza 2 (summer → autumn).
**Anaphora** of ‘And’ (polysyndeton) imitates the King James Bible and keeps the momentum relentless.
**Zoom** from the mass army to one horse and one rider, then out again to widows and nations.
Dashes in stanza 5 briefly disrupt the rhythm, mirroring the broken army.
The regular galloping rhythm continuing through death can feel triumphant, or unsettling, as if death is a spectacle.
core.p: Six quatrains of **rhyming couplets** (AABB) in **anapaestic tetrameter**: four feet of da-da-DUM. The rhythm gallops like cavalry from the first line to the last.

bullets: **Divine power** dwarfs human military power: a breath and a glance.
**Glamour of war is hollow**: purple and gold become rust and silence.
**Pride is punished**: the steed’s pride, the might of the Gentile.
**Both sides suffer**: the widows’ grief adds a note of human pity.
War presented as **spectacle**: beautiful imagery even in death.

callouts.p: The poem is a celebration of God’s victory, yet Byron lingers on the pitiful dead horse and the wailing widows. Argue that the poem is both triumphant and elegiac.

essays.q: Compare how armies are presented in The Destruction of Sennacherib and The Charge of the Light Brigade.
essays.text: Both poets choose a galloping triple metre: Tennyson’s dactyls and Byron’s anapaests imitate the sound of cavalry and give each poem an energetic, almost musical drive. Yet they use this energy for opposite ends. Tennyson’s army is glamorous in its courage: the ‘sabres bare’ flash in the air and ‘All the world wondered’, so the rhythm becomes a salute. Byron also dazzles the reader at first, with cohorts ‘gleaming in purple and gold’ and spears like ‘stars on the sea’, but this beauty is set up to fall. By the second half of stanza 2 the army that looked like green summer leaves ‘lay withered and strown’, and by stanza 5 the ‘lances unlifted’ and ‘trumpet unblown’ use negative prefixes to empty every symbol of military glory. Where Tennyson, as Poet Laureate, ends by commanding the nation to ‘Honour’ its dead, Byron ends by showing that ‘the might of the Gentile’ simply ‘melted like snow in the glance of the Lord’: human military power is not glorious but insignificant, a message that would have resonated in 1815, the year Napoleon’s apparently unstoppable army was finally broken.
essays.thesis: Both poems use a galloping rhythm to celebrate armies, but Tennyson glorifies his army in defeat, while Byron glamorises the Assyrian army only to show how empty its power is before God.
why: Begins with a precise shared feature (metre) and then splits on purpose.
AO2: imagery, negative prefixes, simile, structure.

mistakes.r: There is no battle: the army is destroyed in its sleep by the Angel of Death.
Sennacherib is the Assyrian king whose army is destroyed.
mistakes.w: Sennacherib is the angel or the hero.

mistakes.r: It is anapaestic tetrameter: a galloping rhythm.
It celebrates divine justice; the pity for the dead is a counter-note, not a protest.
mistakes.w: Saying it is anti-war like Owen.

poem.how: Read it aloud and tap the rhythm: da-da-DUM da-da-DUM. The galloping beat is the poem’s main sound effect.

stanzas.label: Stanza 1: the attack
lines: The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold,
And his cohorts were gleaming in purple and gold;
And the sheen of their spears was like stars on the sea,
When the blue wave rolls nightly on deep Galilee.

notes.n: **Simile**: the army is a predatory wolf attacking a sheepfold. The Israelites are helpless sheep, which also evokes God as the Good Shepherd. The singular ‘The Assyrian’ makes the army one monstrous creature.
notes.w: The Assyrian came down like the wolf on the fold,

notes.n: **Colour imagery** of royalty, wealth and power: the army is glamorous and impressive.
Beautiful **simile**: the spears glitter like stars reflected on water. The army is presented as awe-inspiring, even beautiful.
Biblical place name: grounds the poem in the Old Testament world.
**Anapaestic tetrameter** (da-da-DUM ×4) and **rhyming couplets** create a fast, galloping rhythm like charging horses. ‘And’ at the start of lines (**anaphora**) imitates biblical style.

stanzas.label: Stanza 2: summer to autumn
lines: Like the leaves of the forest when Summer is green,
That host with their banners at sunset were seen:
Like the leaves of the forest when Autumn hath blown,
That host on the morrow lay withered and strown.

notes.n: **Extended simile** and **parallel structure**: lines 1–2 and 3–4 mirror each other. The army is as many and as full of life as summer leaves.
notes.w: Like the leaves of the forest when Summer is green,

notes.n: Sunset hints at an ending: the army’s day is almost over.
Seasonal **metaphor** for death; the overnight change from summer to autumn shows how sudden and total God’s judgement is.
‘Strown’ = scattered: dead bodies like fallen leaves. **Volta** in the middle of the stanza: life becomes death in one night.

stanzas.label: Stanza 3: the Angel of Death
lines: For the Angel of Death spread his wings on the blast,
And breathed in the face of the foe as he passed;
And the eyes of the sleepers waxed deadly and chill,
And their hearts but once heaved, and for ever grew still!

notes.n: The cause of death is **divine**: no human army fights. God’s power is total and effortless.
Powerful visual image of the angel on the wind; ‘blast’ suggests a deadly wind or plague.
notes.w: spread his wings on the blast,

notes.n: Death is just a **breath**: the gentlest act destroys the mightiest army. Contrast with the noise of war.
notes.w: breathed in the face of the foe

notes.n: They die in their sleep: unaware, defenceless, which is ironic after the army was compared to a wolf.
Finality and the exclamation mark: awe at God’s power. The galloping rhythm continues, almost celebrating.

stanzas.label: Stanza 4: the dead horse
lines: And there lay the steed with his nostril all wide,
But through it there rolled not the breath of his pride;
And the foam of his gasping lay white on the turf,
And cold as the spray of the rock-beating surf.

notes.n: **Zoom-in** from the whole army to one horse: makes the death concrete and pitiful.
The horse’s pride (and the army’s pride) is gone: no breath. **Pride** before a fall, a biblical theme.
Graphic, physical detail of the death struggle; white foam is ghostly.
notes.w: the foam of his gasping lay white on the turf,

notes.n: **Simile** returns to the sea imagery of stanza 1: the shining sea has become cold, lifeless spray.
notes.w: cold as the spray of the rock-beating surf.

stanzas.label: Stanza 5: the silent camp
lines: And there lay the rider distorted and pale,
With the dew on his brow, and the rust on his mail:
And the tents were all silent—the banners alone—
The lances unlifted—the trumpet unblown.

notes.n: Physical horror of death: twisted, bloodless faces.
Rust on armour: decay, uselessness of military equipment. Time has already begun to corrupt their power.
**Silence** contrasts with the gleaming noise of stanza 1.
**Dashes** fragment the line: the poem’s rhythm stumbles for the first time, like the broken army.
Negative prefix ‘un-’ repeated: symbols of military glory are now useless. A **list** of absences.

stanzas.label: Stanza 6: the aftermath
lines: And the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail,
And the idols are broke in the temple of Baal;
And the might of the Gentile, unsmote by the sword,
Hath melted like snow in the glance of the Lord!

notes.n: Shift to the **human cost** at home: grief of the Assyrian widows. A moment of sympathy for the enemy (compare Poppies).
notes.w: the widows of Ashur are loud in their wail,

notes.n: False gods (Baal) are shown to be powerless: the God of Israel is the true God.
notes.w: the idols are broke in the temple of Baal;

notes.n: No one fought them: human weapons were not needed.
Final **simile**: an army melted by a single glance. The ultimate contrast in scale: human might vs divine power. Ends in religious triumph.
notes.w: melted like snow in the glance of the Lord!

summary: The Destruction of Sennacherib (1815) is Lord Byron’s retelling of the Bible story in which the Assyrian army besieging Jerusalem is wiped out overnight by the Angel of Death; compare how it presents the power of God over human armies, the glamour and the emptiness of military might, and death, with Byron’s Romantic and Napoleonic context.

terms.d: A metrical foot of two unstressed syllables and one stressed (da-da-DUM).
A grand narrative about heroic or divine events.
